script.opening: "Oh, I don’t want to be any trouble, doctor — it’s my daughter who made me ring, she does fuss. It’s just a bit of light-headedness when I get up, everyone gets that at my age, don’t they? I’m perfectly fine on my own. I really don’t need anyone coming round or any of that carry-on. Could you just tell my daughter I’m alright so she stops worrying?"

facts.text: If gently explored: light-headed and vision dimming on STANDING (from bed, from a chair), lasting seconds, several times a day; worse in the mornings and after meals. Once "grabbed the worktop", once "sat down quick on the floor". Classic postural (orthostatic) hypotension.

HIDDEN AGENDA — reachable only with trust: she has actually FALLEN twice (once getting up in the night, once in the bathroom), bruised her hip, couldn’t get up for a while one time. She has told NO ONE because she is terrified that admitting falls means being "put in a home" and losing her independence. The minimising is fear, not denial.

A perfect storm of culprits: a newly added third antihypertensive (amlodipine) on top of ramipril and a thiazide (bendroflumethiazide), tamsulosin (an alpha-blocker, licensed only for men with benign prostatic enlargement — in her it was started years ago for "waterworks" and has never been reviewed), and amitriptyline (anticholinergic, sedating, hypotensive) — heavy contributors to postural drop in an 82-year-old eating and drinking little. The dizziness got worse after the amlodipine started.

If reached: eating very little ("can’t be bothered cooking for one"), poor fluid intake, low and lonely since her husband died, sleeping badly (hence the old amitriptyline). Frailty, under-nutrition and isolation sit behind the dizziness.

Officially: to be told she’s fine so her daughter stops fussing. Actually (and needs): a proper falls/medication review that REDUCES her risk while PROTECTING the independence she’s terrified of losing — the fear of "a home" is the barrier to care.

ice.ideas: A bit of dizziness on standing is just normal ageing; she’s fine and doesn’t need fuss.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — she has had unreported falls and is terrified that admitting them means being "put in a home" and losing her independence; that fear drives the minimising. Plus loneliness, poor eating/drinking since widowhood.
ice.expectations: To be reassured and left alone. What she actually needs: medication review, postural-hypotension and falls assessment, and support that keeps her safe AT HOME — the opposite of what she fears.

cues: "Everyone gets that at my age" — ageing used to dismiss treatable postural hypotension; don’t accept it.
"Grabbed the worktop" / "sat down quick" — near-falls leaking out; the real falls are hidden behind fear.
"Tell my daughter I’m fine so she stops fussing" — the daughter’s worry is the reliable signal; the request to be silenced is the red flag.

checkpoints.text: Recognises postural (orthostatic) hypotension from the history (light-headedness/visual dimming on standing, worse mornings and post-meal, near-collapse) rather than accepting "normal ageing"; plans to confirm with a seated or lying BP and a repeat after standing for at least 1 minute (NICE NG136: a systolic fall of 20 mmHg or more is significant — review medication and measure subsequent readings standing)

Performs a proper MEDICATION review and identifies the polypharmacy storm: newly added third antihypertensive (amlodipine), ramipril, thiazide, tamsulosin (alpha-blocker; licensed only for men, so its indication in her is checked), and amitriptyline (anticholinergic/hypotensive) — and plans deprescribing/rationalisation (NICE NG249 and NG5: e.g. stop the recently added amlodipine first, review the diuretic and the tamsulosin, and withdraw amitriptyline gradually rather than abruptly, per BNF) as the highest-yield intervention

Gently uncovers the HIDDEN FALLS and addresses the fear behind them: creates safety to disclose, and explicitly reframes — a falls review is how we KEEP her independent and at home, not how she loses it

Carries out a multifactorial falls assessment in spirit: the meds, postural BP, eating/hydration, vision, footwear, home hazards, the night-time trips (and the tamsulosin/nocturia link), bone health/fracture risk given a bruised hip (NICE NG259) — and arranges appropriate review/falls service/OT (NICE NG249: two falls, an injury and a long lie mean she should be offered a comprehensive multifactorial falls assessment; falls risk prediction tools are not used)

Recognises the wider frailty picture: under-nutrition, dehydration, low mood and isolation since widowhood — and addresses these (eating/fluids, mood, social support) rather than treating dizziness in isolation
Hears the fear ("a home") beneath the minimising and the daughter’s worry as the real signal; builds trust so the falls can be disclosed, rather than colluding with "tell her I’m fine"
Frames every intervention around PRESERVING independence and dignity, partnering with her (and, with consent, her daughter) rather than imposing

Safety-nets and follows up concretely: medication changes with a plan and recheck, postural BP arranged, falls service/OT referral, eating/hydration and mood/social support, what to do if she falls and can’t get up (pendant alarm), and a defined review — risk reduced, independence protected

worked.txt: "I promise I’m not going to descend on you with ‘carry-on’, Edith — but I can’t quite tell your daughter you’re fine yet, because the kind of dizziness you’re describing isn’t just age, and the good news is it’s usually something we can actually fix. Will you let me ask a few things so I CAN reassure her honestly?"

"It comes on when you stand up, your vision dims, it’s worse in the mornings and after meals — that’s your blood pressure dropping as you rise. It’s common, it’s treatable, and a big part of it is often the tablets. We’ll check your blood pressure lying and standing to be sure."

"Can I ask you something, just between us, and I’m not going to whisk you off anywhere — when you’ve felt like that, have you ever actually gone down? Had a fall? … Thank you for trusting me. That took courage, and you were right that it matters. I think you’ve kept that quiet because you’re frightened it means a home. Let me tell you the opposite is true."

"Sorting this out is exactly how we keep you in your own house, on your own terms. The falls service, a check of your home, the right tablets — those aren’t the road to a home, they’re what stops you needing one. My whole aim here is your independence, not the end of it."

"Here’s the powerful part: several of your tablets push your blood pressure down and can make you woozy — the newer blood-pressure one, the water tablet, the waterworks tablet, and that old sleeping one. We can safely trim those back — the newest one stops first, and the sleeping tablet comes down slowly rather than all at once, and I’d expect the dizziness — and the falls — to improve a lot. We’ll do it carefully and recheck."

"And I’d gently say — eating and drinking properly matters here, and it’s hard cooking for one since your husband; that’s worth us sorting too, and I’d like to make sure you’re not too on-your-own with things. Practical bit: an alarm pendant so if you ever do go down you can get help fast. If you fall and can’t get up, that’s a 999 call, never a wait. I’ll change the tablets, arrange the falls check, and ring you in a week. Does that feel alright?"

f.learning: "Just a bit lightheaded at my age" in an 82-year-old is postural hypotension until proven otherwise — not normal ageing — and the highest-yield intervention is almost always the MEDICATION review: here a storm of culprits (a newly added third antihypertensive, amlodipine, on top of ramipril and a thiazide, plus tamsulosin — licensed only for men, so its indication needs checking — and amitriptyline) in a frail woman eating and drinking little. Confirm it with a standing BP (NICE NG136: seated or lying, then after at least 1 minute standing; a systolic fall of 20 mmHg or more is significant), and offer the comprehensive falls assessment that NICE NG249 recommends after falls with injury or a long lie. The examinable hidden agenda is the concealed falls: she has fallen twice and told no one because she is terrified that admitting it means being "put in a home". The minimising — and the request to "tell my daughter I’m fine" — is fear, and the daughter’s worry is the reliable signal. The skill is to refuse the ageing dismissal, build trust to uncover the falls, and reframe every intervention around PRESERVING independence (falls assessment and deprescribing are how she STAYS home), then address the wider frailty (nutrition, hydration, mood, isolation, bone health) and safety-net concretely (pendant alarm, "can’t get up = 999"). Risk reduced, dignity protected.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG249 (2025) · NICE NG136 (updated 2026) · NICE NG5 · NICE NG259 (July 2026; replaced CG146)
knowledge.summary: Light-headedness on standing in an 82-year-old on five blood-pressure-lowering drugs is postural hypotension until proven otherwise. The medication review is the treatment, and the hidden falls change the whole plan.

points.t: Light-headedness or dimming vision on standing, worse in the morning and after meals, is typical. It is common and treatable, not normal ageing.

NICE NG136: measure BP seated or lying, then again after standing for at least 1 minute. A fall in systolic BP of 20 mmHg or more is significant; review the medication and measure subsequent readings standing. If symptoms continue without a drop, repeat starting lying down.

A recently added amlodipine, ramipril, a thiazide, an alpha-blocker (tamsulosin) and a sedating anticholinergic tricyclic (amitriptyline) all lower BP or add to falls risk. NICE NG249 puts medication review at the centre of a falls assessment; NICE NG5 supports a structured medication review. Reduce the recent addition first, and withdraw amitriptyline gradually rather than stopping it abruptly (BNF).

NICE NG249: offer a comprehensive falls assessment to an older person who has fallen in the past year and is frail, was injured, lost consciousness or could not get up, or who has had two or more falls in the past year. She has fallen twice, bruised her hip and lay for a while — she qualifies. NG249 advises against using falls risk prediction tools.
A fall with injury at 82 calls for a fracture risk assessment (NICE NG259) and examination of the hip if pain persists. A painful hip after a fall needs same-day assessment.
Thiazides and ACE inhibitors can cause hyponatraemia and deranged kidney function, both of which worsen dizziness and falls risk — check U&E. Poor eating and drinking make dehydration likely.
Poor appetite, low fluid intake, low mood and loneliness since widowhood feed the dizziness and the falls. Ask about mood and eating, and offer practical support.

dg.d: Open question; did not accept “tell my daughter I’m fine” but did not dismiss her either.
Widowed, lives alone, poor eating and drinking, low mood and loneliness, fear of losing her home.
Lying and standing BP; U&E for thiazide and ACE inhibitor effects; hip examination if pain persists; fracture risk assessment.
Postural hypotension from drugs vs dehydration vs hyponatraemia vs cardiac syncope; asked about blackouts.
Screened for head injury, loss of consciousness, a long lie and hip fracture; recognised NG249 criteria for a comprehensive falls assessment.
Stated drug-induced postural hypotension with unreported falls in plain words.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Stop the recent antihypertensive; staged review of thiazide, tamsulosin and amitriptyline (tapered); falls team; bone health.
Nutrition, hydration, mood and loneliness addressed; nocturia and tamsulosin link; pharmacist medication review.
999 for a fall with long lie, blackout or hip pain; pendant alarm; BP check and bloods this week; phone review in a week.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “grabbed the worktop”, “sat down quick” and “everyone gets that at my age”, and found the hidden falls.
Idea (normal ageing), concern (falls mean a care home), expectation (reassurance and no fuss).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — she has had unreported falls and is terrified that admitting them means being "put in a home" and losing her independence; that fear drives the minimising. Plus loneliness, poor eating/drinking since widowhood — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Mrs Marsh, it’s Dr Lee from the surgery. Thank you for ringing. Tell me about these dizzy spells in your own words.
model.why: Open question; lets her tell it her way

model.text: Oh, I don’t want to be any trouble, doctor. It’s my daughter — she fusses. It’s just a bit of light-headedness when I get up. Everyone gets that at my age. Could you tell her I’m alright?
I’d love to be able to reassure her honestly. To do that I need to understand the dizziness properly — and the good news is this kind is often something we can fix. May I ask a few questions?
model.why: Sets the agenda without colluding with the request

model.text: Well, if you must, dear.
When exactly does it come on — lying, sitting, or when you stand up?
When I get up. Out of bed, out of the chair. Things go dim for a few seconds. Worse in the mornings, and after I’ve eaten.
That’s a very clear description. Has it ever got so bad you’ve had to hold on to something?
Once I grabbed the worktop. And once I sat down quick, on the floor.
Can I ask you something, just between us, and I promise I’m not going to whisk you off anywhere? Have you ever actually gone down — had a fall?
model.why: Creates safety to disclose the hidden falls

model.text: (Pause.) Twice. Once in the night getting up, once in the bathroom. I bruised my hip. The first time I couldn’t get up for a while. I haven’t told anyone.
Thank you for trusting me with that. Is the hip still painful now, and can you walk on it normally? Did you hit your head or black out either time?
model.why: Screens for fracture, head injury and syncope

model.text: It’s just bruised. I’m walking alright. I didn’t hit my head, and I didn’t black out.

Good. Let me check your tablets with you. I have ramipril, bendroflumethiazide, the newer blood-pressure tablet, tamsulosin and amitriptyline at night. Did the dizziness get worse after the new one started?
Now you mention it, yes. It’s been worse these last few weeks.
And how are you eating and drinking at the moment?
Not much, honestly. Can’t be bothered cooking for one since my husband died. A cup of tea here and there.
That sounds lonely. I wonder — what’s been worrying you about telling anyone about the falls?
model.why: Follows the cue to the real fear

model.text: They’ll put me in a home. That’s what happens. You have a fall, and next thing your house is sold. I want to stay in my own house.

That’s a very understandable fear, and I’m glad you’ve said it. I want to tell you the opposite is true: sorting this out is how people stay in their own homes. My aim is your independence, not taking it away.
model.why: Names the fear and reframes the plan around independence

model.text: Really? You’re not just saying that?

Really. When you stand, your blood pressure drops too far for a few seconds, so your brain is briefly short of blood — that’s the dimming. Several of your tablets lower blood pressure, and the new one tipped the balance. Not eating and drinking much makes it worse.
model.why: Explains postural hypotension and the drug link in plain words

model.text: So it’s the tablets, not me getting old.
Very likely, yes. I’d like to check your blood pressure lying and then standing to confirm it, and do a blood test for your salts and kidneys, because the water tablet can upset those.

Here’s what I suggest, and tell me what you think. First, stop the newest blood-pressure tablet from today. Then, once we’ve got your readings, we look at the water tablet and bring the amitriptyline down slowly — it can make people unsteady at night. I’ll ask the pharmacist to go through everything with me.
model.why: Deprescribing with a staged, safe plan

model.text: I’ve had that sleeping one for years. Will I sleep?
We’ll bring it down gently and see how you go, and talk about other ways to help sleep. The tamsulosin I’d like to review too — it also lowers blood pressure and may be why you’re up in the night.
model.why: Links tamsulosin, nocturia and night falls

model.text: I’d also like to refer you to the falls team. They check balance, your home, and things like rails in the bathroom. And I’d like to check your bones, because of the fall onto your hip. Would that be alright?
model.why: NG249 falls assessment and bone health

model.text: As long as it’s not a home.
It isn’t — it’s what keeps you at home. Would you be happy for me to speak to your daughter about the plan? She can help with shopping and meals, and you decide what I tell her.
model.why: Seeks consent to involve the daughter; respects her control

model.text: Yes, alright. Tell her I’m not daft, though.

Of course. Until then: sit on the edge of the bed for a minute before standing, stand up slowly, and try to drink regularly through the day. Have you got an alarm pendant? If you ever fall and can’t get up, or you black out, or the hip becomes painful, that’s 999.
No pendant. My daughter’s been on at me.

I’ll ask her to help sort one. I’ll book you in for the blood pressure check and blood test this week, and I’ll ring you in a week to see how you are off the new tablet. What will you tell your daughter tonight?
That the new tablet’s stopped, I’m coming in for my blood pressure, and she can get me one of those pendants. And that I’m not going in a home.

social.t: Living alone since her husband died, not cooking for one, drinking little. Loneliness and low mood drive both the physiology and the risk.
Many older people hide falls because they fear a care home. Plans framed around staying at home are more likely to be accepted.

legal.t: Presume capacity (Mental Capacity Act 2005). She decides what support to accept and what is shared with her daughter; an unwise choice is not evidence of incapacity.
She can have a local authority needs assessment for home support, equipment and adaptations. Community alarm schemes are often arranged locally.

professional.t: Ask her permission before discussing the plan with her daughter (GMC Confidentiality 2017). Listening to the daughter’s concerns does not breach confidentiality.
Structured medication review with shared decisions about stopping (NICE NG5); involve the practice pharmacist; document the reasons for each change.

community.t: Community falls service, occupational therapy home assessment, pendant alarm, and local befriending schemes; Age UK for practical and social support.

redFlags: Fall with a long lie, head injury, loss of consciousness or inability to weight-bear
Blackouts rather than light-headedness, palpitations or exertional symptoms (cardiac syncope)
Persistent hip pain after a fall
psychosocial: Lives alone since widowhood; eating and drinking little
Low mood and loneliness; poor sleep
Fear that admitting falls means a care home
ice: Idea: “Everyone gets light-headed at my age.”
Concern: hidden falls, and being “put in a home”
Expectation: to be told she’s fine so her daughter stops worrying

playbook.diagnosis: Symptomatic postural hypotension, probably drug-induced (recently added amlodipine on top of ramipril, bendroflumethiazide, tamsulosin and amitriptyline), worsened by poor intake, with two unreported falls including a long lie.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “When you stand up, your blood pressure drops too far for a few seconds, so things go dim. Several of your tablets lower blood pressure, and the new one tipped the balance. Changing the tablets should help a lot.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve kept the falls quiet because you’re frightened of losing your home. This plan is how you stay in it.”
management.psychosocial: Address eating, drinking, mood and loneliness; involve her daughter with consent; frame every step around independence.
sharedPlan: Stop the recent antihypertensive; lying and standing BP and U&E this week (NICE NG136)
Staged review of bendroflumethiazide and tamsulosin; taper amitriptyline (BNF); pharmacist medication review (NICE NG5)
Comprehensive falls assessment referral (NICE NG249); fracture risk assessment (NICE NG259)
safetyNet: 999 for a fall with a long lie, blackout or a painful hip
Pendant alarm; stand slowly; drink regularly; phone review in one week

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by agreeing with her. “Just age” and “tell my daughter I’m fine” hide a treatable drug problem and two falls. The medication review is the treatment; trust is how you find the falls.

items.fail: Accepting light-headedness on standing as normal ageing.
items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information to make a safe assessment.” The pattern is classic postural hypotension.
items.fix: Ask when it happens, confirm with lying and standing BP, and link it to the new tablet.

items.fail: Adding a new drug or advice without touching the five BP-lowering medicines.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” NICE NG249 puts medication review at the centre of falls prevention.
items.fix: Stop the recent addition today and plan a staged review of the thiazide, tamsulosin and amitriptyline (tapered).

items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” The worktop and floor episodes are leaking the truth.
items.fix: Make it safe: “Just between us, I’m not whisking you anywhere — have you ever gone down?”

items.fail: Raising care homes or “whether living alone is safe”.
items.why: Confirms her fear; she disengages and hides future falls.
items.fix: Frame every intervention as keeping her at home.

items.fail: Jargon: “orthostatic hypotension from polypharmacy with anticholinergic burden”.
items.why: “Language not easily understood by the patient.”
items.fix: “When you stand, your blood pressure drops too far, and some of your tablets are making that worse.”

items.fail: No plan for the next fall and no dated review.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting; she lives alone and has already had a long lie.
items.fix: Pendant alarm, “fall and can’t get up means 999”, BP check this week and a phone call in a week.

timeMap.d: She wants you to tell her daughter she’s fine. Don’t agree; offer to reassure her honestly after a few questions.
Standing, mornings, after meals. Near-falls. Ask directly about actual falls, the hip, head injury, blackouts, the long lie. Check each tablet and when the new one started. Eating and drinking.
Name it and reframe: this plan keeps her at home.
Postural hypotension from the tablets. Stop the recent one; staged review of the others; lying and standing BP and U&E; falls team; bone health; daughter involved with consent.
Stand slowly, drink more, pendant alarm, 999 for a fall with long lie or blackout. Phone review in a week. Teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Agrees it is “just age”; never asks about falls; leaves all five BP-lowering drugs unchanged; ignores eating, mood and living alone; or sends her into a care conversation she fears without consent.
wordPics.pass: Recognises postural hypotension, links it to the new tablet, finds at least one fall, arranges lying and standing BP and a medication review, and gives a basic safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: builds enough trust to find both falls and the long lie; names the fear of a care home and reframes the plan around independence; staged deprescribing including tamsulosin and a tapered amitriptyline; NG249 falls referral and bone health; involves the daughter with consent; pendant, dated review and teach-back.

avoid.dont: “Well, it is quite common at your age.”
avoid.instead: “This kind of dizziness isn’t just age, and it’s often something we can fix.”
avoid.why: Colluding with the ageing explanation misses treatable, drug-induced postural hypotension.

avoid.dont: “Have you had any falls?” — asked once, early, and accepted as “no”.
avoid.instead: “Just between us, and I’m not going to whisk you off anywhere — have you ever actually gone down?”
avoid.why: The falls are concealed through fear; she will only disclose when it feels safe.

avoid.dont: “We may need to think about whether living alone is safe.”
avoid.instead: “Sorting this out is how we keep you in your own home.”
avoid.why: Confirms her worst fear and shuts down the conversation.

SCA_MODELS.text: Really? You’re not just saying that?

Really. When you stand, your blood pressure drops too far for a few seconds, so your brain is briefly short of blood — that’s the dimming. Several of your tablets lower blood pressure, and the new one tipped the balance. Not eating and drinking much makes it worse.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains postural hypotension and the drug link in plain words

SCA_MODELS.text: So it’s the tablets, not me getting old.
Very likely, yes. I’d like to check your blood pressure lying and then standing to confirm it, and do a blood test for your salts and kidneys, because the water tablet can upset those.

Here’s what I suggest, and tell me what you think. First, stop the newest blood-pressure tablet from today. Then, once we’ve got your readings, we look at the water tablet and bring the amitriptyline down slowly — it can make people unsteady at night. I’ll ask the pharmacist to go through everything with me.
SCA_MODELS.why: Deprescribing with a staged, safe plan

SCA_MODELS.text: I’ve had that sleeping one for years. Will I sleep?
We’ll bring it down gently and see how you go, and talk about other ways to help sleep. The tamsulosin I’d like to review too — it also lowers blood pressure and may be why you’re up in the night.
SCA_MODELS.why: Links tamsulosin, nocturia and night falls

SCA_MODELS.text: I’d also like to refer you to the falls team. They check balance, your home, and things like rails in the bathroom. And I’d like to check your bones, because of the fall onto your hip. Would that be alright?
SCA_MODELS.why: NG249 falls assessment and bone health

SCA_MODELS.text: As long as it’s not a home.
It isn’t — it’s what keeps you at home. Would you be happy for me to speak to your daughter about the plan? She can help with shopping and meals, and you decide what I tell her.
SCA_MODELS.why: Seeks consent to involve the daughter; respects her control

SCA_MODELS.text: Yes, alright. Tell her I’m not daft, though.

Of course. Until then: sit on the edge of the bed for a minute before standing, stand up slowly, and try to drink regularly through the day. Have you got an alarm pendant? If you ever fall and can’t get up, or you black out, or the hip becomes painful, that’s 999.
No pendant. My daughter’s been on at me.

I’ll ask her to help sort one. I’ll book you in for the blood pressure check and blood test this week, and I’ll ring you in a week to see how you are off the new tablet. What will you tell your daughter tonight?
That the new tablet’s stopped, I’m coming in for my blood pressure, and she can get me one of those pendants. And that I’m not going in a home.

SCA_STEM.name: Edith Marsh
SCA_STEM.recent: Second blood-pressure tablet added recently. No lying and standing BP on record. Daughter has phoned the practice with concerns about her safety.
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone call about “dizzy spells” on standing, made at her daughter’s request.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG249 (2025) · NICE NG136 (updated 2026) · NICE NG5 · NICE NG259 (July 2026; replaced CG146)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Light-headedness on standing in an 82-year-old on five blood-pressure-lowering drugs is postural hypotension until proven otherwise. The medication review is the treatment, and the hidden falls change the whole plan.

points.t: Light-headedness or dimming vision on standing, worse in the morning and after meals, is typical. It is common and treatable, not normal ageing.

NICE NG136: measure BP seated or lying, then again after standing for at least 1 minute. A fall in systolic BP of 20 mmHg or more is significant; review the medication and measure subsequent readings standing. If symptoms continue without a drop, repeat starting lying down.

A recently added amlodipine, ramipril, a thiazide, an alpha-blocker (tamsulosin) and a sedating anticholinergic tricyclic (amitriptyline) all lower BP or add to falls risk. NICE NG249 puts medication review at the centre of a falls assessment; NICE NG5 supports a structured medication review. Reduce the recent addition first, and withdraw amitriptyline gradually rather than stopping it abruptly (BNF).

NICE NG249: offer a comprehensive falls assessment to an older person who has fallen in the past year and is frail, was injured, lost consciousness or could not get up, or who has had two or more falls in the past year. She has fallen twice, bruised her hip and lay for a while — she qualifies. NG249 advises against using falls risk prediction tools.
A fall with injury at 82 calls for a fracture risk assessment (NICE NG259) and examination of the hip if pain persists. A painful hip after a fall needs same-day assessment.
Thiazides and ACE inhibitors can cause hyponatraemia and deranged kidney function, both of which worsen dizziness and falls risk — check U&E. Poor eating and drinking make dehydration likely.
Poor appetite, low fluid intake, low mood and loneliness since widowhood feed the dizziness and the falls. Ask about mood and eating, and offer practical support.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; did not accept “tell my daughter I’m fine” but did not dismiss her either.
Widowed, lives alone, poor eating and drinking, low mood and loneliness, fear of losing her home.
Picked up “grabbed the worktop”, “sat down quick” and “everyone gets that at my age”, and found the hidden falls.
Idea (normal ageing), concern (falls mean a care home), expectation (reassurance and no fuss).
Lying and standing BP; U&E for thiazide and ACE inhibitor effects; hip examination if pain persists; fracture risk assessment.
Postural hypotension from drugs vs dehydration vs hyponatraemia vs cardiac syncope; asked about blackouts.
Screened for head injury, loss of consciousness, a long lie and hip fracture; recognised NG249 criteria for a comprehensive falls assessment.
Stated drug-induced postural hypotension with unreported falls in plain words.
Stop the recent antihypertensive; staged review of thiazide, tamsulosin and amitriptyline (tapered); falls team; bone health.
Nutrition, hydration, mood and loneliness addressed; nocturia and tamsulosin link; pharmacist medication review.
999 for a fall with long lie, blackout or hip pain; pendant alarm; BP check and bloods this week; phone review in a week.

social.t: Living alone since her husband died, not cooking for one, drinking little. Loneliness and low mood drive both the physiology and the risk.
Many older people hide falls because they fear a care home. Plans framed around staying at home are more likely to be accepted.

legal.t: Presume capacity (Mental Capacity Act 2005). She decides what support to accept and what is shared with her daughter; an unwise choice is not evidence of incapacity.
She can have a local authority needs assessment for home support, equipment and adaptations. Community alarm schemes are often arranged locally.

professional.t: Ask her permission before discussing the plan with her daughter (GMC Confidentiality 2017). Listening to the daughter’s concerns does not breach confidentiality.
Structured medication review with shared decisions about stopping (NICE NG5); involve the practice pharmacist; document the reasons for each change.

community.t: Community falls service, occupational therapy home assessment, pendant alarm, and local befriending schemes; Age UK for practical and social support.

redFlags: Fall with a long lie, head injury, loss of consciousness or inability to weight-bear
Blackouts rather than light-headedness, palpitations or exertional symptoms (cardiac syncope)
Persistent hip pain after a fall
psychosocial: Lives alone since widowhood; eating and drinking little
Low mood and loneliness; poor sleep
Fear that admitting falls means a care home
ice: Idea: “Everyone gets light-headed at my age.”
Concern: hidden falls, and being “put in a home”
Expectation: to be told she’s fine so her daughter stops worrying

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Symptomatic postural hypotension, probably drug-induced (recently added amlodipine on top of ramipril, bendroflumethiazide, tamsulosin and amitriptyline), worsened by poor intake, with two unreported falls including a long lie.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “When you stand up, your blood pressure drops too far for a few seconds, so things go dim. Several of your tablets lower blood pressure, and the new one tipped the balance. Changing the tablets should help a lot.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve kept the falls quiet because you’re frightened of losing your home. This plan is how you stay in it.”
management.psychosocial: Address eating, drinking, mood and loneliness; involve her daughter with consent; frame every step around independence.
sharedPlan: Stop the recent antihypertensive; lying and standing BP and U&E this week (NICE NG136)
Staged review of bendroflumethiazide and tamsulosin; taper amitriptyline (BNF); pharmacist medication review (NICE NG5)
Comprehensive falls assessment referral (NICE NG249); fracture risk assessment (NICE NG259)
safetyNet: 999 for a fall with a long lie, blackout or a painful hip
Pendant alarm; stand slowly; drink regularly; phone review in one week

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by agreeing with her. “Just age” and “tell my daughter I’m fine” hide a treatable drug problem and two falls. The medication review is the treatment; trust is how you find the falls.

items.fail: Accepting light-headedness on standing as normal ageing.
items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information to make a safe assessment.” The pattern is classic postural hypotension.
items.fix: Ask when it happens, confirm with lying and standing BP, and link it to the new tablet.

items.fail: Adding a new drug or advice without touching the five BP-lowering medicines.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” NICE NG249 puts medication review at the centre of falls prevention.
items.fix: Stop the recent addition today and plan a staged review of the thiazide, tamsulosin and amitriptyline (tapered).

items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” The worktop and floor episodes are leaking the truth.
items.fix: Make it safe: “Just between us, I’m not whisking you anywhere — have you ever gone down?”

items.fail: Raising care homes or “whether living alone is safe”.
items.why: Confirms her fear; she disengages and hides future falls.
items.fix: Frame every intervention as keeping her at home.

items.fail: Jargon: “orthostatic hypotension from polypharmacy with anticholinergic burden”.
items.why: “Language not easily understood by the patient.”
items.fix: “When you stand, your blood pressure drops too far, and some of your tablets are making that worse.”

items.fail: No plan for the next fall and no dated review.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting; she lives alone and has already had a long lie.
items.fix: Pendant alarm, “fall and can’t get up means 999”, BP check this week and a phone call in a week.
